item.title: When the state becomes a family business. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Democracy can persist through elections, legislative bodies, and formal constitutions, yet it can simultaneously erode the essential public dimension of governance. When familial ties, political allegiance, and private wealth dictate access to power and the allocation of public resources, democracy risks devolving into an empty framework encasing a privatized political economy. Bangladesh is not an exception.
“Nepotocracy” extends beyond the mere favouring of relatives by individual politicians; it characterizes a systemic phenomenon where dynastic relationships serve as conduits for the perpetuation of political influence.
Kleptocracy, by contrast, describes a regime in which public authority is systematically exploited for personal financial gain.
In Bangladesh, nepotism and kleptocracy are significantly prominent, diminishing public trust in political parties and the government.
The peril escalates when these two systems reinforce one another. Familial networks can safeguard access to political authority, while wealth accrued through political channels can further entrench and replicate these familial structures.
Consequently, a political-economic feedback loop emerges, in which the distinctions between familial, state, and private capital become increasingly indistinct.
Are elections enough?
Contemporary political discourse frequently positions elections as the cornerstone of democracy. However, elections alone do not ensure democratic governance, especially in countries with limited law enforcement and widespread political fragmentation, such as Bangladesh.
A nation may conduct regular elections, yet political competition can remain profoundly imbalanced. It can boast a constitutional framework while powerful entities operate through informal networks that bypass formal processes.
Parliamentary structures may exist, but legislators often find themselves beholden to party leadership or influential political patrons. The judiciary may exist, yet political influence can compromise its independence.
Thus, the critical concern transcends the mere existence of democratic institutions; it lies in their functional integrity.
The World Bank's political-economy framework provides valuable insights in this regard, telling us how skewed power distributions can foster exclusion, capture, and clientelism, ultimately eroding effective governance, equity, and developmental progress.
This distinction is paramount. Democracy cannot merely be viewed as an assembly of institutional frameworks. It must also be understood as a dynamic system of relationships through which power is allocated and exercised.
When a select political family or interlinked elite networks monopolize these relationships, a veneer of formal democracy can coexist with substantive socio-economic inequality, and we have seen this practice in Bangladesh since its independence in 1971.
From nepotism to nepotocracy
Nepotism is a well-known phenomenon wherein individuals in positions of power extend preferential treatment to family members, close associates, and stakeholders with shared interests.
This practice often aims to optimize wealth accumulation and profits, frequently through questionable or unethical operations. It highlights the implications of familial and social ties in decision-making processes, potentially undermining fairness and meritocracy in both economic and organizational contexts.
While nepotism is rampant in political structures, where familial relationships heavily influence appointments, succession, economic advantages, and access to state resources, nepotocracy is something larger.
There is a difference between isolated instances of favouritism, which may breach public-sector integrity but don't destabilize the political system, and systemic nepotism, where family ties continually affect political parties, government agencies, and institutions, ultimately perpetuating political power.
Does political power begin to acquire a hereditary character?
Yes, familial networks can be important for political success. "Political capital" means the trust and influence a person has in politics. Politicians use it to gain support for their ideas, influence public opinion, or achieve goals.
Family members often build connections over time, allowing them to pass down financial support from one generation to the next. Relationships with government officials, businesses, and media can also boost these advantages.
This dynamic does not necessarily eliminate electoral processes. Instead, elections unfold within a framework in which certain political actors have disproportionately more resources and networks than their counterparts.
This scenario poses a complex democratic challenge: What are the implications when political competition remains formally inclusive, yet access to political authority becomes increasingly concentrated among a limited number of familial dynasties?
Modern nepotocracy in Bangladesh
Sociologist Max Weber provides a valuable framework for understanding authority structures, distinguishing between rational-legal authority and patrimonial authority. In a rational-legal bureaucracy, authority is institutional rather than personal; established rules and qualifications fill positions, and decision-making follows formal protocols.
In the context of Bangladesh, the concepts of patrimonial authority and modern nepotocracy resonate strongly with the political and administrative landscape. The country has a long history of political dynasties in which loyalty to specific leaders or families plays a critical role in governance.
In many cases, political power is less about democratic processes and more about personal connections and kinship ties, which reflects the principles of patrimonial authority.
Governance in Bangladesh is hybrid, blending formal democratic structures with traditional patronage networks. Although the constitution supports democratic principles, political appointments often rely on personal loyalties rather than expertise, leading to ineffective leadership.
This undermines public trust and productivity. Despite grassroots movements advocating change, newly elected administrations often continue their predecessors' autocratic practices, hindering institutional reform and democratic accountability. In public administration, political connections often compromise recruitment despite a facade of merit-based processes.
The state consequently operates according to two competing logics: Formal rational-legal institutions and informal patrimonial networks.
The tension between those two systems is at the heart of the problem in any country, especially in Bangladesh.
When political power becomes economic capital
In Bangladesh, kleptocracy is particularly relevant when examining the intersection of political power and economic resources. The dynamics described earlier can be observed in how political officeholders often prioritize personal enrichment over public welfare.
In Bangladesh, governance challenges are often highlighted by allegations of corruption and mismanagement, in which a select few in power misappropriate public resources.
Political patronage plays a crucial role in distributing government contracts, land, and natural resources. For example, infrastructure projects intended for public benefit often end up bolstering the interests of politically-connected groups, illustrating how public assets are redirected for private gain.
Moreover, the persistent interests that shape state policy in Bangladesh often favour elite networks, reinforcing systemic inequalities.
The contradiction becomes evident as citizens see institutions formally designated as public entities while the economic benefits that should accrue to the broader population increasingly concentrate within a narrow circle of the political elite.
This situation reflects a shift in the allure of political office in Bangladesh -- from a genuine commitment to serve the public good to a pathway for accessing rents and economic opportunities.
Political engagement can indeed resemble a financial investment for many politicians and their affiliates, shifting the focus away from serving constituents and toward maximizing personal or collective financial benefits.
Consequently, this analysis of kleptocracy not only sheds light on the structural vulnerabilities within Bangladesh's political and economic systems but also emphasizes the need for reforms that prioritize accountability and transparency to reclaim public resources for the benefit of all citizens.
The family and the money trail
Nepotism and corruption present serious dangers, particularly when they reinforce each other. Imagine a political system where trusted family members and close associates hold key positions. These positions grant them access to vital information, public contracts, regulatory decisions, and government resources. As a result, economically-influential groups benefit, concentrating private wealth.
This wealth can then be utilized to back political groups, finance electoral campaigns, and maintain patronage systems. Consequently, the political structure becomes increasingly fortified as the cycle continues.
This dynamic can be briefly outlined as follows:
Family political dominance → loyal appointments → institutional takeover → preferential access to public assets → wealth gathering → political funding and patronage → strengthened political connections → further institutional takeover.
Understanding this cyclical pattern is essential to grasp how corruption endures even after individual officials are removed. The problem often goes beyond specific corrupt politicians; it involves an institutional framework that consistently incentivises political actors to repeat such actions.
From bribery to state capture
Over the years, Bangladesh has faced significant challenges related to governance, characterized by various forms of corruption, including bribery and systematic manipulation of state mechanisms.
Bribery often manifests in public services, where officials may accept kickbacks to expedite processes or bypass regulations. This creates an environment where the rule of law is undermined, and ordinary citizens may struggle to access essential services without resorting to illicit practices.
However, the more insidious issue of state capture is particularly relevant to understanding the dynamics of power in Bangladesh.
Prominent political actors have been known to influence the formulation of laws and regulations to benefit their interests or those of their supporters.
For example, the crafting of contracts in infrastructure projects or natural resource extraction can be tailored to favour companies with political ties, often marginalizing competition and compromising fair business practices.
Moreover, the privatization processes in Bangladesh have raised concerns about the transfer of state assets to politically-connected businesses, sometimes disguised as legitimate transactions.
This not only consolidates power among elite factions but also perpetuates economic inequalities, undermining democratic governance and accountability.
As a result, state capture in Bangladesh shows how the exploitation of public resources can occur within a framework that appears legal, creating an illusion of propriety while eroding public trust and stifling economic development.
Understanding this connection can foster a critical examination of the systemic issues at play and encourage reforms aimed at restoring integrity and accountability in governance.
Nepotocracy thus threatens meritocracy, where social connections can overshadow qualifications and competence, leading to disengagement from public institutions and a focus on relationships over productivity.
This shift fosters corruption as a new norm, distorting competitive environments and leading to institutionalized democratic inequality, where political and economic inequalities reinforce each other.
Kleptocracy operates globally, complicating efforts to combat corruption because illicit wealth moves across borders.
While global financial integration can facilitate development, it also hinders national governments in tracking and recovering corruptly obtained assets. Addressing kleptocracy requires international cooperation among states, financial institutions, and civil society.
Recommendations
Nepotocracy and kleptocracy thrive in Bangladesh due to a complex interplay of political vulnerabilities, social dynamics, and cultural norms. Addressing these issues requires strengthening institutions, promoting transparency, and shifting societal attitudes toward corruption and nepotism.
Only through concerted efforts at various levels can substantial progress be made in combating these prevalent systems.
Strengthening democratic institutions is crucial. Enhancing the independence and capacity of bodies like the judiciary and electoral commissions can help uphold the rule of law free from political interference. Promote transparency and accountability by establishing mechanisms for public access to government contracts and financial disclosures, supported by independent audits of public spending.
Encouraging civic engagement is another vital component. Fostering an active civil society and public awareness campaigns can empower citizens to participate in governance and hold their leaders accountable.
Additionally, implementing anti-nepotism laws with clear guidelines will help ensure that merit prevails over familial connections in public appointments.
Political reforms should aim to democratize party structures and introduce term limits to reduce the concentration of elite power. Lastly, enhancing economic opportunities for all, regardless of family ties, will help create a more equitable society.
By addressing these interrelated issues, Bangladesh can pave the way for genuine democratic governance that prioritizes the common good and fosters sustainable development.
Dr ASM Anam Ullah (PhD) is an Australian senior academic, editor, human rights activist, political analyst, and OHS and industrial relations expert.

item.title: Exploring our diplomatic ties. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
We are encouraged by the recent diplomatic engagements exploring a potential free trade agreement (FTA) between Bangladesh and Uzbekistan.
Bangladesh’s economic diplomacy has long remained narrowly tethered to a handful of traditional Western and regional markets, leaving our export basket and strategic partnerships overly vulnerable to external shocks.
To that end, ties with nations such as Uzbekistan signal a refreshing and long-overdue evolution in our foreign policy.
Reaching beyond our usual comfort zones to forge robust trade and investment corridors is, at this point, the logical and sensible approach.
As Bangladesh navigates arguably its most challenging economic period in its five and a half decades of being a sovereign state, with slowing domestic growth and mounting global trade pressures, diversifying our international partnerships must become a central pillar of statecraft.
Central Asia offers untapped potential, rich resources, and expanding consumer markets that can absorb our manufactured goods, particularly ready-made garments, while opening new channels for agricultural, technological, and infrastructural collaboration.
Establishing direct connectivity, streamlining business-to-business contacts, and pursuing bilateral FTAs with nations outside our traditional orbit will not only provide much-needed resilience to our external sector but also offer genuine space for further growth and potential innovation.
However, high-level diplomatic handshakes and exploratory talks must quickly translate into concrete action. Historically, our trade ambitions have often stalled in bureaucratic hesitation, failing to move past preliminary memorandums.
The government must therefore aggressively follow through on these emerging ties, and beyond our positive talks with Uzbekistan, continue to explore strengthening ties with other non-traditional partners across the globe.
Diversifying our trade geography, reducing reliance on saturated markets, and actively pursuing economic diplomacy should, over time, lead to long-term prosperity. It is time for us to continue casting a wider net on the global stage.

item.title: Helping teachers keep up. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
It goes without saying that in an era where students navigate complex digital landscapes with ease, educators can no longer rely on chalkboard methods of the past.
To that end, we agree with Education Minister ANM Ehsanul Hoque Milon’s recent call for teachers to master technology and artificial intelligence (AI) to keep pace with digitally fluent students.
To maintain academic relevance, our teaching corps must indeed embrace technological innovation, critical research, and inclusive classroom practices. All of that is a given, and difficult to argue against.
However, telling teachers to adapt without giving them the tools to do so is an exercise in futility. That, unfortunately, has been the reality for some time now when it comes to our education.
Ambitious directives that have been handed down from administrative boardrooms are meaningless if the ground-level reality of our schools and education institutions remains woefully underfunded and disregarded.
Instructors - particularly in rural and under-resourced institutions - grapple with chronic shortages of basic digital infrastructure, inadequate computer labs, unreliable internet, and zero structured training modules.
Expecting such educators to independently bridge the digital divide while burdened by heavy workloads and administrative neglect is completely unrealistic and shows a lack of awareness on the part of the authorities regarding the reality of such educators.
If the government is serious about modernizing our education system, rhetoric must be matched with substantial state investment. Meaningful digital transformation will require comprehensive, continuous, and well-funded professional development programs that equip every teacher with hands-on AI and technology training.
Educators must embrace the challenge of lifelong learning, but the state must provide the robust institutional backing, resources, and institutional support required to make that growth possible.
We cannot build a future-ready education system by demanding modern outcomes from neglected, unsupported teachers.

item.title: The death of browsing. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
There was a time when retail therapy lived up to its name.
Walking into a store, whether a neighbourhood superstore or a trendy lifestyle outlet like Shwapno or Miniso, offered a quiet escape.
A shopper could drift along the aisles, pause to inspect an unfamiliar gadget, read product labels, or simply indulge in the mindless joy of browsing.
It was an unhurried, low-pressure experience where decision-making happened at the consumer’s own pace.
Today, that tranquil space has been replaced by a subtle, relentless tension.
The moment you step through the entrance of a modern retail outlet, you are greeted not with subtle hospitality, but with a sharp, chorus-like shout of "Welcome!" designed less to make you feel comfortable and more to signal that you are now under active surveillance.
From that second onward, the modern retail experience becomes an exercise in evasion.
Staff members shadow your every movement. "What are you looking for, ma'am?" "Have you tried this new lotion?" "We have a promotion on this item today."
What line management calls "proactive customer assistance" feels almost like continuous harassment.
Instead of creating an environment conducive to organic discovery, this aggressive push marketing destroys the mental space needed to make buying decisions -- and ultimately hurts the merchant’s bottom line.
Retail operations often operate on a flawed metric: Equating floor staff proximity with superior customer service.
Management training modules frequently mandate that employees approach every customer within seconds of entry, pitch active promotions, and remain within arm’s reach to offer continuous assistance.
In business theory, this is intended to maximize basket size, prevent shoplifting, and project attentiveness.
In practice, however, it fundamentally misunderstands consumer psychology.
Modern retail thrives on passive browsing -- the psychological phenomenon where a customer enters a shop with no specific intent to buy, but leaves with a basket full of unneeded items simply because they were allowed the time and mental peace to admire them.
When a sales associate physically shadows a shopper, the consumer's cognitive load spikes.
The brain shifts from a state of open curiosity to defense.
You can no longer look at an aesthetic desk lamp or an interesting cosmetic product and wonder how it fits into your life; your mental bandwidth is entirely consumed by formulating polite ways to decline unwanted sales pitches or plotting an exit strategy from the aisle.
The immediate result of this invasive hovering is "cart abandonment" -- not on a website, but in real life.
Consider a typical visit to a grocery chain’s frozen food aisle: A shopper enters looking for chicken salami.
Finding the shelf empty, they are immediately cornered by a promoter persistently pushing frozen parathas.
Despite multiple polite refusals, the sales pitch continues unabated. Overwhelmed and irritated, the shopper flees the section entirely to escape the social pressure.
It is only after returning home that they realize they could have easily substituted the salami with chicken sausages -- a cross-sell opportunity completely destroyed by overzealous push tactics.
The cost of short-term conversions
Why do retail businesses double down on tactics that alienate their customer base? The answer lies in misaligned key performance indicators (KPIs).
On paper, push marketing generates measurable short-term wins.
An aggressive floor associate can occasionally pressure an indecisive customer into buying a featured product just to end the uncomfortable interaction.
In daily sales reports, this looks like a successful conversion attributable to staff initiative.
What management fails to track, however, are the long-term losses:
In an era where e-commerce offers friction-free, silent shopping from the comfort of one's couch, physical brick-and-mortar stores have precisely one major advantage: Tactile experience and environment .
When stores ruin that environment with noise and physical boundary-crossing, they hand their entire market share directly to online platforms.
Redefining in-store engagement
Fixing the retail environment does not require abandoning customer support altogether; it requires transitioning from push assistance to permission-based service.
Retail leaders aiming to rebuild customer loyalty and maximize true retention can consider several structural remedies:
Customer service was never meant to be an exercise in coercion.
At its core, good retail service is about removing friction, not creating it.
When businesses mistake constant interruption for dedication, they trade sustainable customer retention for short-sighted sales pushes.
The modern consumer does not want to be chased down an aisle or pressured into buying frozen bread when they come for cold cuts.
They want the freedom to browse, evaluate, and enjoy the physical space at their own pace.
Until retail operations learn to respect the quiet psychology of shopping, their floor staff will continue to drive away the very customers they are paid to welcome.
Wafiur Rahman looks after the business desk at Dhaka Tribune.

item.title: Building workplaces free from sexual harassment. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Bangladesh has taken important steps on sexual harassment at work. The Labour Act addresses aspects of the issue, and Bangladesh has ratified ILO Convention No 190 (C190) on Violence and Harassment. With the Labour rules under review, the challenge is to turn legal commitments into a coherent system that workers can trust, organisations can implement and regulators can enforce.
This is first a matter of rights. No one should have to trade dignity or safety for work. C190 recognizes the right to a world of work free from violence and harassment and calls for prevention, protection, enforcement, and remedies.
It is also a productivity issue. The International Labour Organization reports that workplace sexual harassment cost the world $2.6 billion in lost productivity in 2018, alongside $0.9bn in other financial costs.
Unsafe workplaces contribute to absenteeism, turnover, and disengagement; poorly handled complaints can escalate into disputes and reputational damage. Prevention and effective response are not simply compliance costs; they are part of good governance and risk management. The business case reinforces the rights-based case; it does not replace it.
The development sector has an equal stake. Donors expect credible protection from sexual exploitation, abuse and harassment (PSEAH) systems: Safe reporting, competent investigations, non-retaliation, and support.
For the government, this means giving effect to Bangladesh’s international commitments. Bangladesh ratified C190 on 20 November 2025; it enters into force for Bangladesh on 20 November 2026. Its gender-responsive approach spans prevention, enforcement, remedies, investigation, training, and social dialogue. The rules reform is an opportunity to make these principles workable.
What needs to happen next?
The aim should be a coherent system, not more requirements for their own sake.
First , clarify the relationship between Sections 23, 24, 332, and 332A. Sections 23 and 24 provide the misconduct and disciplinary framework, while Sections 332 and 332A address prevention and the complaints committee.
The law should clarify how complaints and investigations connect with disciplinary proceedings: Who investigates, who decides, what safeguards apply, and how remedies follow.
Investigators should establish findings on the evidence; the appropriate authority should decide on action in accordance with law and due process. The committee need not replace disciplinary authority, but the pathway from complaint to decision and remedy must be clear. If the Act does not support it, amendment may be needed.
Second , operationalize Section 332. The rules should translate employers’ preventive duties into practical expectations on policies, risk assessment, training, reporting channels and protection from retaliation.
Third , give Section 332A clear procedures. The Act provides for a five-member complaints committee, with a majority of women, a woman chair and two members from organizations working on gender and sexual violence. The rules should clarify its mandate, independence, timelines, confidentiality, reporting lines, and safeguards against interference.
Fourth , establish an end-to-end process for receiving concerns, assessing safety, selecting an investigator, managing conflicts of interest, assessing evidence, deciding on action, informing parties, and providing remedies. It should address harassment involving supervisors, contractors, clients, and service providers.
Fifth , protect complainants, witnesses, and committee members against retaliation while balancing confidentiality with the respondent’s right to know and respond. An allegation that cannot be established is not, for that reason alone, malicious.
Finally , make the rules workable for multinationals, factories, NGOs, and small enterprises. Systems may differ in scale, but all should meet core principles: Prevention, safe reporting, fair investigation, accountability, and remedy. The Act should establish rights and duties; rules provide the machinery but cannot fill substantive gaps.
Why does this matter?
Workers should be able to speak up without risking livelihood, dignity or safety. For organizations, a fair process can address concerns before they escalate.
Trade unions gain confidence that workers can raise concerns without retaliation; employers’ organizations gain a more consistent playing field. The government can show that its commitments are more than words, while development organizations sustain donor confidence.
For businesses, the issue extends across supply chains. Buyers want evidence that worker voice, grievance mechanisms, and remedies function in practice, not simply that a policy exists.
There is also a market-access dimension. The EU is Bangladesh’s largest trading partner, and textiles are a major part of its imports from Bangladesh.
After LDC graduation, Bangladesh is due to retain Everything But Arms preferences for at least three years under the revised EU GSP framework and may seek GSP+. The framework emphasizes human rights, labour rights, and good governance.
From December 14, 2027, the EU Forced Labour Regulation will prohibit products made with forced labour from being placed on or made available in the EU market. Harassment is not itself forced labour, but violence, intimidation, and abuse of vulnerability can be relevant to wider forced-labour risks. Market access depends on price, quality, and delivery, but also on evidence that labour rights are respected.
This is not simply about compliance; it is about good governance and good business. A credible system protects rights, reduces productivity losses, supports responsible supply chains, gives effect to international commitments, and helps safeguard market access.
“Zero tolerance” should not mean zero complaints. A workplace with no complaints may be safe, or it may be one where people do not feel safe enough to speak. Zero tolerance should mean zero tolerance for harassment, retaliation, and inaction.
Bangladesh has moved towards legal reform. The next step is to make the law and rules work together. That is where the real test of reform will lie.
Jenefa Jabbar is Barrister-at-Law and Principal, JJC. This article has been developed through Bangladesh Institute of Labour Studies- BILS and GoodWeave International under the project titled “Promoting Living Wage, Labour Rights, and Human Rights Due Diligence in Bangladesh.”

item.title: ​​Libya: Racism and ‘resettlement’ conspiracies fuel fear among Tripoli’s migrants. [ middleeasteye ]
item.description:
​​Libya: Racism and ‘resettlement’ conspiracies fuel fear among Tripoli’s migrants

Submitted by Driss Rejichi on Thu, 10/15/2026 - 13:08
A surge in anti‑migrant protest is reshaping life for Sub‑Saharan people already living in precarious conditions
Libyans outside the International Organization for Migration in Tripoli demand action against irregular migrants and refugees, on 16 June 2026 (Mahmud Turkia/AFP)
Off

1 October was supposed to be the “deadline” for foreign migrants in Tripoli. In the weeks leading up to it, dozens of groups and pages on social media urged Libyans to take to the streets in openly xenophobic protests.

Featuring racist slurs and depictions of Sub-Saharan, Arab and Asian migrants, the widely shared Facebook posts were intimidating.

The migrant rights group Refugees in Libya even reported receiving a handwritten threat targeting “black people”, delivered with a bullet, days before the planned protest.

Eventually, the demonstrations barely materialised, overshadowed by a large teachers’ strike over unpaid salaries directed at Abdul Hamid Dbeibah, head of the Government of National Unity (GNU), which rules the west of the divided country.

Still, dozens of protesters took to the streets in Tripoli on 2 and 9 October, rallying in Martyrs’ Square and chanting “Libya for Libyans” and “No to resettlement”.

Similar demonstrations have taken place several times a month in central Tripoli since April, steadily fuelling hostility towards migrants.

With nearly 700,000 Sub-Saharan Africans living in the Tripoli area, including some 335,000 Sudanese refugees fleeing the war, the Libyan capital has become a major hub for migrants seeking to reach Europe.

Between January and August, Libya was the departure point for around 80 percent of the 19,000 migrants who reached Italy through the Mediterranean. More than 90 percent of departures occurred from western Libya, particularly the coastline between Tripoli and Zuwara, long known as a major launch point for boats.

Attacks on migrant aid agencies

Already exposed to smuggling networks, arbitrary detention, kidnapping, torture and slavery – “systematic human rights violations and abuses”, according to the UN – as well as violent interception at sea, migrants now face growing threats in their homes and workplaces.

“I feel that Libyans are increasingly allowed to do whatever they want to us, without obligation to abide by the law,” Albert G, a 37-year-old Sierra Leonean living in eastern Tripoli, told Middle East Eye.

“Not only will torture and imprisonment continue to be a reality for migrants, which is already a well-known problem, but it also adds more common difficulties when there is no way for us to enter the public places or look for work to survive.”

‘I feel that Libyans are increasingly allowed to do whatever they want to us, without obligation to abide by the law’

– Albert, Sierra Leonean migrant

Albert says hostility began rising with the first protests in spring and became genuinely frightening at the start of summer.

In June, large crowds of Libyans protested for the first time against what they called a “resettlement plan”, allegedly orchestrated by the United Nations to prevent migrants from leaving the country.

Despite firm denials from the International Organization for Migration (IOM) and the UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), hundreds of protesters blocked the UNHCR headquarters in Tripoli on 4 June, accusing international agencies of trying to alter Libya’s demographics.

The protests were accompanied by anti‑migrant violence and waves of arrests of Sub-Saharans by the police and armed factions aligned with the interior ministry across several western Libyan cities, prompting many Sub‑Saharan people to remain indoors for days.

Although the unrest subsided during the summer, small gatherings and sporadic incidents continued.

On 7 September, tensions escalated when a group of Libyans stormed an IOM Migrants' Response Centre in western Tripoli. No casualties were reported, but the attack deeply unsettled the Sub‑Saharan community.

“If the authorities can allow an IOM camp to be attacked, many lives will be impacted because there will be no safe place for migrants,” Albert said.

Authorities accused of ‘complacency’

Following the incident, the GNU stated that “the right to peaceful protest can never justify assault, vandalism or threats to life”, warning that perpetrators could face legal action.

Asked by MEE about steps taken since the attack, the interior ministry failed to respond.

Meanwhile, popular Facebook and X pages created in spring remain active, spreading hate speech and promoting calls for mobilisation. Groups such as “Libyan News – No to the Resettlement In Libya” (76,000 members) and “The Tripoli Activists Movement” (39,000 members) continue to share hateful content targeting migrants daily.

Libya: Video reveals young Ethiopian woman being tortured for ransom 
Read More »

The degree of coordination behind the movement and its origin remain unclear. A BBC investigation in August found that the June protests were fuelled by online rumours.

On the ground, public figures such as lawyer Thuraya al-Tuwaibi and journalist Salma al‑Shaab have repeatedly led protests – which they call "peaceful" – reinforcing their momentum.

“These campaigns are still ongoing, even though they are based on false and misleading information,” Ahmed Hamza, a Libyan human rights activist, told MEE.

“The actions of those advocating for or coordinating this criminal movement constitute criminal acts punishable under the Libyan Penal Code,” he added.

Hamza pointed to “a state of complacency, complicity, and suspicious silence from the interior ministry and other authorities”.

Migrants echo this sentiment, saying that while the GNU allows them to live and work in Libya – and sometimes even employs them – it has never guaranteed their safety in Tripoli.

‘I have never felt safe in Libya’

Kingsley (pseudonym), a Cameroonian refugee who has lived in Tripoli for four years, told MEE he has “never felt safe in Libya”.

Arrested twice by security forces in 2024 and 2025, the young man says he was released only after paying money to what he describes as his “kidnappers”. Beyond criminal gangs, armed groups affiliated with state institutions have been repeatedly accused of holding civilians to ransom.

“Now, I see the vast majority of Libyans as a threat,” Kingsley said.

‘Now, I see the vast majority of Libyans as a threat’

– Kingsley, Cameroonian refugee

While Sub‑Saharan Africans remain the main targets of online hate campaigns, some posts also target Palestinian, Syrian and Bangladeshi communities – particularly present in eastern Libya but increasingly visible in Tripoli.

Migrants also report more frequent violations of their rights and disrespect from locals amid the hostile climate, even when incidents are not directly linked to the anti‑resettlement movement.

“Last week, I worked at a construction site for two days and received no money. I had to go home on an empty stomach,” Albert said.

New protest dates have not been announced yet, but tensions around the anti‑resettlement movement continue to simmer, raising concerns that the situation could worsen.

“Authorities must assume their responsibilities. Matters could escalate and get out of control,” Hamza warned.

So far, the hostile climate has not prompted large numbers of migrants to leave Tripoli, but some are considering it. The IOM operates voluntary return programmes that assisted around 16,000 migrants in 2025, while the Libyan authorities deported more than 37,000 last year.

“Even if the situation is terrible there too, I would rather be in Tunisia, or Algeria,” Albert said. “I don’t know what the coming months have in store for us here.”

item.title: Sympathy alone will not extinguish flames. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Our hearts go out to the grieving families of the victims who lost their lives in the horrifying fire at the Tup-Tup Resort in Cox’s Bazar. That unsuspecting vacationers seeking peace in our country’s most popular tourist district should instead be trapped in an inferno is a heartbreaking tragedy.
Yet, beyond offering sympathy, we must confront, once again, the criminal negligence and systemic failure that allow these death traps to operate with impunity.
The revelation that, as per the fire service department, the resort lacked a valid fire safety license -- and had explicitly ignored official warnings issued in June -- transforms this tragedy from an accident into a predictable, preventable crime.
Constructing a multi-storey commercial establishment out of highly combustible bamboo and wood without mandatory suppression infrastructure, emergency exits, or staff training is a direct gamble with human lives. That resort personnel reportedly fled the scene as the flames spread only highlights a complete breakdown of duty of care.
This tragedy exposes a chronic failure of regulatory enforcement which is not limited to just factories and warehouses. Official warnings and post-disaster probes are utterly meaningless if authorities allow unlicensed, unsafe establishments to continue.
It goes without saying that a full investigation is necessary. Moreover, we need a sweeping, unyielding audit of every hotel, resort, and commercial venue in tourist zones that must be carried out without delay.
Unlicensed and non-compliant properties must be shut down, and the owners and regulators who ignored explicit safety warnings must face prosecution to the fullest extent of the law.
Until accountability is enforced with zero tolerance, commercial greed and administrative apathy will continue at the expense of innocent lives that will continue to burn.

item.title: There can be no development without employment. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The latest findings from the International Monetary Fund (IMF), revealing that nearly 29% of highly educated youth in Bangladesh are unemployed, while half of those employed work in jobs far below their qualifications, tells us that when it comes to job creation and employment, we are, without question, a profound socio-economic failure.
For a nation that has been banking on its demographic dividend to propel it into future prosperity for some time now, these numbers are not only depressing, but simultaneously a damning indictment of our archaic educational framework and haphazard labour market.
When nearly a third of our brightest minds are left idle or underemployed, it is certainly not just a statistical concern but a squandering of national potential. It is the type of squandering that threatens long-term economic stagnation for this country.
The root of this crisis is a glaring, persistent mismatch between what our academic institutions teach and what the modern economy actually demands. For decades, traditional degrees have churned out graduates disconnected from industrial reality, while technical, vocational, and digital skills training remain woefully neglected.
Compounding this, our labour markets remain choked by an overwhelming informal sector that lacks job security, formal contracts, and career progression, while bureaucracy, favouritism, and connections keep out worthy candidates from ever taking on roles fit for their qualifications.
Treating youth unemployment as a temporary inconvenience or relying on fragmented, cosmetic training programs will no longer suffice. Turning our demographic growth into a genuine economic advantage requires immediate, aggressive structural overhaul.
For that to happen, the state, in partnership with private industry, must radically modernize our curricula to align with market demands, prioritizing technical competency, critical thinking, and digital fluency. Public investment must also prioritize creating high-productivity jobs while providing robust support for innovative enterprises.
We cannot preach national development while forcing our graduates into despair and underemployment. Without equipping our youth with meaningful, dignified employment, there can be no development.

item.title: Why columns matter. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
One of my newspaper columns changed how the British government works.
OK, changed in a pretty small way, but change it it did.
Which is a useful answer to the question posed by HM Nazmul Alam in this newspaper .
Why do we write opinion columns, why do we bother? As we say in Britain, today's newspapers are, after all, tomorrow's wrappers for the fish and chips.
We might provide some passing amusement to readers but are we actually important? Do we change the world at all?
So, an example from my own life. My writing life if you prefer.
It's an obvious observation that there are a lot of people demanding that taxes should be higher. Usually, taxes on other people should be higher.
But there are some who insist that the government having more money would make the world a better place. So, I wondered about this. I went to the UK Treasury and asked them whether anybody had made extra, voluntary, tax payments last year because they thought this way.
That no one had asked this before became clear very quickly. For no one knew. Not only that, the Treasury itself thought the idea wholly ridiculous.
It took them a few months to find out, but eventually they were able to tell me that in the tax year 2005, there had been five voluntary donations. Donations -- four of those donating were dead, leaving bequests. From which we can derive that there was one whole person in the country of the 70 million at the time who thought that the government having more money was so important that they voluntarily sent in more tax than they had to pay.
This is not grand evidence of the desire of everyone to pay more tax, of course, despite the very high number of people who demanded that taxes should be higher.
So, I wrote my column, The Times published it in 2006. I thought it was a very good joke, and I cashed my cheque for having written it.
As far as I was concerned, that was that. Well, except for dragging that example out now and again when there was one or another group demanding that they all be taxed more. For there are such groups.
Patriotic Millionaires is one of them. Rich people who demand that they be taxed more because they're rich. To which a perfectly sensible, even sufficient, answer is that you can pay extra tax, go ahead. Isn't it amazing how none of them do?
A number of people have, over the years, repeated my column, including the numbers for different tax years. I've not been keeping track but I think I'm right in saying that never has the number gone beyond a dozen of those voluntary, extra, taxpayers.
So far so, just me and my little joke. But a few weeks back, those Patriotic Millionaires demanded, again, that they be taxed more. The answer from the government was that you can pay extra tax, if you wish, and they referred to the government webpage which explains how to do it . That response, that webpage, stems directly from that column I did two decades ago.
But is it true that writing a newspaper column can indeed change the world?
Obviously, we're not going to bring about peace, love, and understanding for all forever. But it might well be possible to make a little change, here or there.
In my professional work at a think-tank, I've been a part of more substantial changes too. But yes, columns matter. And it's not the ones we think either.
I really was trying to make a joke about the difference between the public calls and the private actions, and I was doing so in order to do nothing more than gain a few pounds sterling to spend on my own desires.
One final thing. A little thing for any journalist out there interested in finance. Repeat the article for Bangladesh. We all know -- and can probably identify -- those who insist that taxes should be higher.
So, go and ask the authorities how many people pay higher than legally demanded taxes. Find out -- how many people made donations to the government last tax year? The article comparing that to how many call for higher taxes will be published. If you really work at it, you can do it anew each year too.
No, I'll not try to charge a royalty on the idea -- I stole it from an American, about the US, in the first place. They've been running an account called “Gifts to the United States” since 1843. It's never received more than a handful of millions of dollars in any one year.
People just don't believe in higher taxes enough to pay them when they don't have to. And that? That's a really useful little lesson from a newspaper column.
Tim Worstall is a senior fellow at the Adam Smith Institute in London.

item.title: Revenge is not a development strategy. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Two World Bank reports, published less than 11 months apart, illustrate the increasing fragility of Bangladesh's development gains.
The November 2025 Poverty and Equity Assessment documented a decline in national poverty from 37. 1% in 2010 to 18. 7% in 2022.
The Bangladesh Development Update, released on October 6, 2026, presents a troubling reversal: National poverty is estimated at 22.5% in FY 2025-26 and projected to reach 22.8% in FY 2026-27.
The latest update also estimates that approximately 2.1 million additional people fell below the international poverty line of $3 per day during FY 2025-26.
This is a distinct measure from the national poverty rate. Both indicators point to deteriorating household welfare, although neither represents a new household survey count. This distinction is important when using these figures to assess government performance.
The central question is whether Bangladesh can pursue accountability without undermining productive businesses and the livelihoods they support. When political retaliation damages factories or obstructs legitimate commerce, workers bear costs that have not been imposed by any court.
A fair assessment requires acknowledging that the crisis did not begin in August 2024. Inflation, foreign exchange shortages, and import restrictions had already weakened the economy.
Banking vulnerabilities accumulated over many years due to weak oversight, connected lending, and governance failures. The poverty assessment also found that growth had become less inclusive after 2016. Recent global energy disruptions have added further pressure.
However, inherited conditions do not absolve the government of responsibility. Governments must be assessed on whether their actions contain existing weaknesses or exacerbate them.
The World Bank identifies financial fragility, energy constraints, weak revenue mobilization, and uncertainty as obstacles to recovery. Protecting lawful business activity and maintaining public order are essential components of an effective response.
Growth slowed from 5.8% in FY 2022-23 to 4.2% in FY 2023-24, then to 3.5% in FY 2024-25, and is estimated at 3.4% in FY 2025-26. The slowdown therefore began during the Awami League regime.
Moreover, FY 2025-26 spans both the interim and the elected government, with the latter assuming office in February 2026. Attributing the entire year's performance to either administration would misrepresent the chronology.
Nevertheless, the destruction of industrial assets after August 2024 deserves direct scrutiny. The looting and arson at Gazi Tires in Rupganj on August 25, 2024 became a disturbing example of the failure to protect a business associated with a former minister.
Reports of missing people require careful investigation; they should not be presented as a confirmed death toll. The destruction itself, and its consequences for employment, are sufficient grounds for concern.
A March 5, 2025, Prothom Alo report recorded 95 permanent factory closures across major industrial areas during the preceding seven months, affecting 61,881 workers.
Its explanation extended beyond political violence: Financial distress, insufficient orders, attacks on politically-connected businesses, and owners going into hiding all contributed. The report identified 33,244 job losses across 14 factories in Beximco Industrial Park. These losses are included in the broader total and should not be counted as an additional figure.
This evidence supports criticism of inadequate protection and industrial disruption. However, it does not establish that every closure resulted from retaliation. Maintaining this distinction strengthens the argument by focusing attention on failures that authorities could reasonably have prevented or mitigated.
An owner accused of corruption should be subject to investigation, asset recovery where justified, and a fair trial. Employees, suppliers, and customers should not automatically lose their livelihoods or contracts.
Where legally permissible and commercially feasible, professional administration or restructuring can preserve a viable enterprise while the courts determine liability. These arrangements must protect creditors and prevent the concealment or diversion of assets.
Nor should the preservation of employment serve as a justification for rescuing every indebted conglomerate with public funds. Some businesses may be insolvent or reliant on privileges that cannot continue.
The objective should be orderly restructuring, transparent decision-making, and payment of workers’ lawful dues. Political identity should neither confer immunity nor substitute for evidence.
Achieving this requires decisions at the level of individual enterprises. Authorities should distinguish funds suspected of being criminal proceeds from those necessary for lawful operations. Restrictions should be justified, proportionate, and subject to review.
Workers need clear information on wages and compensation, while lenders require reliable financial statements and a viability assessment.
Without this discipline, a campaign against wrongdoing can spread losses throughout an entire supply chain and undermine confidence in legitimate enforcement.
The broader deterioration in public order reinforces this concern. In its year-end 2025 reporting, Ain o Salish Kendra recorded at least 197 deaths from mob violence during that year and reported at least 293 since the interim administration began.
The latter was a cumulative figure reported before that administration ended, not a final count for its entire tenure. These deaths demonstrate a serious failure of protection, although they cannot all be classified as political retaliation.
Human Rights Watch’s January 2025 report also documented the resurgence of abusive security practices and reprisals against individuals perceived to support the Awami League. Its warnings about arbitrary arrests and indiscriminate criminal complaints underscore the importance of due process.
Accountability loses credibility when allegations supplant investigation or when individuals are treated as guilty by association.
Economic consequences arise through identifiable channels. Damage to factories disrupts production and deliveries. Uncertain legal treatment may discourage lending and investment. Workers who lose wages reduce their spending, affecting shops, transport operators, and other local businesses.
These mechanisms provide compelling reasons to protect enterprises, although the World Bank’s aggregate figures do not quantify the distinct contribution of political retaliation.
The investment indicators are concerning. Private sector credit growth fell to its lowest level in 33 years. Net foreign direct investment declined by 15% in FY 2025-26, while new equity investment fell by 70. 3%.
Weakness in the financial sector, energy shortages, and global conditions also influence these outcomes. These figures are warning signs of a challenging investment environment, rather than evidence of a single political cause.
The earlier poverty assessment recorded nearly two million fewer employed people between 2023 and 2024 and projected a further decline of 0.8 million in 2025. That projection should not be treated as a subsequently verified outcome. Its broader message remains relevant: Weakening employment and purchasing power threaten households with limited capacity to absorb shocks.
There are also achievements to acknowledge. Remittances reached $35.6 billion in FY 2025-26, reserves improved, and average inflation eased from 10% to 8.7%.
More transparent recognition of problem loans is necessary, although the reported non-performing loan ratio of 33.2% in June 2026 demonstrates the scale of the remaining repair effort. Macroeconomic stabilization is valuable, but it must translate into productive investment and employment.
The elected government now bears responsibility for recovery. It should protect viable firms through lawful restructuring, investigate industrial arson regardless of political affiliation, and review cases through independent scrutiny of the evidence.
Bank restructuring requires credible deadlines and a fair allocation of losses. Reliable energy supply and stronger revenue collection should also form part of the recovery agenda.
Households need protection while these reforms take effect. About half of the poorest remain outside social protection programs. The World Bank estimates that consolidating food subsidies and combining the Family Card with better targeting of existing cash programs could lift millions out of poverty.
Bangladesh need not choose between justice and jobs. It must pursue justice through institutions capable of protecting both public funds and lawful livelihoods.
The promise of dignity after the uprising cannot be fulfilled if ordinary workers repeatedly bear the costs of their employers' politics.
The writer is a US-based policy analyst and freelance consultant on financial risk management.

item.title: Fazl clarifies he criticised policies, not institutions after ministers allege he sought 'share' in KP governance. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Jamiat Ulema-i-Islam-Fazl (JUI-F) chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman on Saturday clarified that his party’s remarks regarding the country’s security situation were directed at policies, not institutions, and termed the allegations levelled against him by federal ministers as character assassination.

A day earlier, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, without naming anyone, had claimed that a “head of a party” was “extremely upset” about not being appointed the governor of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. The remarks came after Fazl accused the Centre of depriving the provinces of their rights and raised doubts over its reasoning behind imposing governor’s rule that there was a lack of cooperation on counterterrorism.

Earlier on Saturday, State Minister for Interior Tallal Chaudhry also rebuked the JUI-F chief for reportedly seeking his “share” in KP’s governance following the imposition of governor’s rule and an emergency in the province. Other federal ministers have also taken exception to Fazl’s remarks.

Addressing a press conference in Lahore on Saturday, Fazl stressed that his party’s criticism was directed at policies, not institutions, and was intended to bring about corrective action rather than undermine the sacrifices made in the fight against terrorism.

The senior politician called for an in-camera session of Parliament to review the country’s security situation and formulate a consensus-based policy to combat terrorism.

“Our only question is why the country has failed to eliminate terrorism. Let us sit together and find out why. Parliament is the most appropriate forum to discuss the issue and make decisions. Instead of ridiculing politicians, the government should take them on board in this fight so that we can move forward together,” he said.

“If Parliament is supreme, why are decisions taken in Rawalpindi while Parliament is simply told to follow them?” he remarked. “The issue is that this government is powerless. Decisions are taken somewhere else, and it implements them obediently,” he alleged.

The JUI-F maintained that Parliament should review the security situation and that the nation should be taken into confidence. If the public was expected to support the fight against terrorism and those engaged in it, he argued, the government should explain its decisions rather than impose “unilateral measures”.

Fazl reiterated his objection to the imposition of emergency rule in KP or any other part of the country. Recalling his family’s opposition to emergency rule in Balochistan during the 1970s, he said his father had resigned when the government of Zulfikar Ali Bhutto imposed it in the province.

He described the recurrence of such measures as unfortunate, pointing out that the PP had repeatedly been associated with their imposition.

Questioning the rationale behind the emergency, governor’s rule and deployment of troops in KP, Fazl asked why the province should face such treatment when Balochistan was also grappling with the same level of terrorist violence, if not more.

The JUI-F chief urged the government to develop a shared national narrative and a consensus-based counterterrorism strategy instead of questioning his party’s position.

He went on to ask why the government engaged in negotiations with the PTI, which had been in power in KP, if the party was accused of supporting terrorists. “On top of it, both (the PTI and the government) say that they had reached a consensus on all points.”

Fazl then highlighted that around 250 of his party workers had lost their lives in terrorist violence, arguing that their sacrifices should not be ridiculed or overlooked. “How can a party whose members have laid their lives be accused of supporting terrorists?” he asked.

He also questioned why he was being singled out for criticism when political leaders, including former prime minister Nawaz Sharif, had at various times disagreed with the military leadership.

Earlier on Saturday, addressing the media in Jaranwala, Chaudhry said, “I am upset. We did not expect Maulana sahab […] to consider this as spoils of war and seek his share in the absence of a PTI government in the province.”

He also alleged that the PTI founder had allowed the TTP to open offices in Peshawar.

During his address, Chaudhry also criticised the PTI, showing a press release issued by the TTP that condemned the dismissal of the party’s government.

Meanwhile, speaking at a press conference in Sialkot, Defence Minister Khawaja Asif criticised the JUI-F chief for constantly “targeting” the country’s security forces.

He declared that the sacrifices made by the security forces, officers, and the public in the fight against terrorism were “matchless”.

This politician, Naqvi alleged, had remained “dependent on the establishment for decades to advance his political career”.

“These are the same politicians who remained in politics for decades with the support of the establishment, and this politician even relied on the establishment to arrange air tickets for the members of his party,” he further alleged.

She said it was not expected of a senior politician such as him to support those who facilitate terrorism — an apparent reference to the PTI, which the Centre accuses of backing terrorism.

The move has drawn criticism from the opposition, including Fazl, as well as Mehmood Khan Achakzai and Raja Nasir Abbas of the Tehreek-i-Tahafuz-i-Ayin-i-Pakistan.

In the days preceding the imposition of governor’s rule in KP, political tensions between the Centre and the opposition — including the PTI which was in power in KP — had remained high since jailed former prime minister Imran Khan’s party announced a protest march to Islamabad to demand his release.

Intense negotiations between the two sides a week before the imposition of governor’s rule had failed to yield any results, while Fazl was cast as the man who could defuse heightening tensions between the Centre and the PTI. Both sides had held separate meetings with Fazl, reportedly for his intervention to help break the deadlock in the negotiations.

item.title: Bangladesh is battling measles. It's a 'real warning' to other nations. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Bangladesh is battling to contain the world’s worst measles outbreak, a crisis exacerbated by weak data, inadequate outreach and vaccination gaps that experts say offers a warning to other nations about the deadly risk of falling immunisation rates.

Bangladesh, whose routine vaccination programme faltered in 2025, reported 202,000 suspected measles cases – 22,000 of them laboratory-confirmed – since the start of the outbreak in mid-March to October 9, the World Health Organisation said. That’s more suspected cases than any other country this year.

So far, 1,147 people have died of the highly contagious disease, with 94 per cent of reported deaths among children under five years old, the WHO said.

Bangladesh’s experience shows the challenge of containing an outbreak when vaccination coverage falls below 95pc, a level the WHO says is needed to prevent outbreaks. Bangladesh almost achieved that in recent years but in 2025 coverage dropped.

A Reuters review of WHO documents, alongside interviews with more than a dozen scientists, health workers and officials, shows Bangladesh was also hampered in its emergency response by data that left out millions of children, shortcomings in preparation and a failure to reach enough parents.

“This is a real warning to every country,” said Mark Jit, a WHO vaccine adviser and professor at the School of Global Public Health at New York University.

Preventing an outbreak through vaccinations was easier, cheaper and safer than responding to an emergency, he said.

“The response will stop the outbreak eventually, but in the meantime, many will have had measles, and some will have died,” he said.

Ziauddin Hyder, special assistant on health affairs to Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, told Reuters in September the government was doing everything it could to end the outbreak. The government did not respond to further questions sent in October for this article.

‘They came only after i Buried my son’

In the northeast Sylhet region, one of the worst-hit areas in the nation of 178 million people, two-year-old Arman Hossain died unvaccinated in July, 24 hours after admission to hospital for treatment paid for by selling the family’s three-wheeled auto rickshaw. His unvaccinated four-year-old sister survived.

His father Amin Mia, 26, said no health workers came to their remote village in Sylhet to offer vaccinations in time. “They came only after I buried my son,” he said.

Measles usually kills two or three people in every 1,000 cases, the WHO says, but the disease can be more deadly in poorer nations because of factors such as malnutrition.

In the town of Chhatak, also in the Sylhet region, the daughter of 30-year-old carpenter Humayun Rashid died unvaccinated in June aged nine months. Labiba Akter could have received an inoculation in April when an emergency programme lowered the vaccination age to six months from nine.

“No health worker came to tell us,” her father said.

In a report published in July this year, WHO and UNICEF estimated first-dose coverage in 2025 had fallen to 90pc, while second-dose coverage was 86pc, several percentage points below the 95pc needed for herd immunity.

The report also raised questions about the quality of official data on vaccinations for measles and other diseases for the years 2023 to 2025.

It said preliminary figures sometimes showed numbers of those inoculated exceeded 100pc of those targeted, indicating mistakes in counting doses or target numbers.
